definitions.definition: For a periodic integrable f, hat f(k)=(2*pi)^(-1) integral_0^(2*pi) f(x) exp(-i*k*x) dx. The transform extends by completion to Sobolev spaces and by distributional duality. Reality means hat f(-k)=conjugate(hat f(k)); mean zero means hat f(0)=0.

definitions.type: family of Fourier Sobolev spaces and norms
definitions.definition: For real s, <k>=(1+k^2)^(1/2), ||f||_(H^s)^2=sum_(k in Z) <k>^(2*s)|hat f(k)|^2. H^s is the completion of trigonometric polynomials, interpreted as distributions for negative s; L2=H^0 with the normalized spatial norm. On mean-zero functions ||f||_(dot H^s)^2=sum_(k!=0)|k|^(2*s)|hat f(k)|^2. Time suprema use continuous representatives and derivative norms essential suprema. For sequences x, ||x||_(ell2)^2=sum_k |x(k)|^2; ell1 uses sum_k |x(k)|. Frequency projections P_{<=A}, P_{>A} retain respectively |k|<=A and |k|>A.
S_t=exp(-t*partial_x^3), hat(S_t f)(k)=exp(i*t*k^3)*hat f(k), for every real t.
P0 f=hat f(0), identified with the constant function.
Dinv=D^(-1)=partial_x^(-1): its multiplier is (i*k)^(-1) at k!=0 and zero at k=0. D^(-2)=Dinv composed with Dinv. Spatial derivatives use multiplier i*k.
J_t(f,g)=S_(-t) P[(S_t Dinv f)(S_t Dinv g)].
For I=[a,b] with 0<=a<=b, Cint_I(f,g,h)=integral_I S_(-t) P{P[(S_t f(t))(S_t g(t))]*(S_t Dinv h(t))}dt; time-independent inputs are read as constant paths.
p_star=23/14. For an interval I of length at most one, ||f||_X(I)=||f||_(L^infty(I;L2))+||partial_t f||_(L^infty(I;H^(-p_star))).

output.statement: S_t is unitary in every H^s, preserves reality and zero mean. On mean-zero inputs, uniformly in real t: ||Dinv f||_(H^1)+||Dinv f||_infty<=C||f||_2; ||B_t(f,g)||_(H^(-23/14))<=C||f||_2||g||_2; ||J_t(f,g)||_(H^1)<=C||f||_2||g||_2. For every A0 in H^1, ||A0||_infty<=C||A0||_(H^1). For A0,B0 in H^1, ||A0 B0||_(H^1)<=C||A0||_(H^1)||B0||_(H^1). Also ||Dinv P(FG)||_2<=C||F||_2||G||_2, ||A0||_(H^(-23/14))<=||Dinv A0||_2 for mean-zero A0, and ||J_t(A0,B0)||_2<=C||Dinv A0||_2||B0||_2 whenever the right side is defined. For smooth mean-zero paths f,g on [a,b], integral_a^b B_t(f,g)dt=(1/3)[J_t(f,g)]_a^b-(1/3)integral_a^b[J_t(f',g)+J_t(f,g')]dt. Moreover J is symmetric and integral_I J_t(B_t(f,g),h)dt=Cint_I(f,g,h). These identities hold stepwise for piecewise smooth paths, and Stage_(n,tau)(t;f)=[J_s(f,f)]_(s=n*tau)^t/6.

argument.text: Orthogonality of exp(i*k*x) in normalized measure gives the L2 Fourier norm identity on polynomials; completion gives it on L2. Unimodularity and conjugate symmetry of exp(i*t*k^3) give unitarity, reality and mean preservation of S directly in Fourier coefficients. Cauchy-Schwarz gives ||Dinv f||_infty<=(sum_(k!=0)k^(-2))^(1/2)||f||_2, and ||Dinv f||_(H^1)<=sqrt(2)||f||_2. More generally H^1 embeds in L^infty by the same summable reciprocal weights. For A0,B0 in H^1, the product rule together with this embedding gives ||A0 B0||_(H^1)<=C||A0||_(H^1)||B0||_(H^1), first on polynomials and then by density. Apply this to the two inverse derivatives to obtain the J bound. The Fourier coefficient of a product of two L2 functions is bounded by the product of their L2 norms by Cauchy-Schwarz. Therefore ||B_t(f,g)||_(H^(-p_star))^2<=||f||_2^2||g||_2^2 sum_(k!=0) k^2<k>^(-2*p_star), and this series converges because p_star=23/14>3/2. The same coefficient bound with sum k^(-2) gives ||Dinv P(FG)||_2<=C||F||_2||G||_2. On mean-zero coefficients <k>^(-p_star)<=|k|^(-1), so the negative-norm comparison follows. In J_t(A0,B0), bound its first inverse derivative in L2 and its second in L^infty to get the asymmetric bound. All constants are uniform in t since S is an isometry. Bounded-product extensions follow by the displayed estimates and density.

For smooth mean-zero paths f,g the nonzero kth Fourier coefficient of J_t(f,g) is sum_(a+b=k) exp(-i*3*k*a*b*t)(i*a)^(-1)(i*b)^(-1) hat f(a)hat g(b). Differentiating the phase contributes 3*i*k times the product coefficient. Thus partial_t J_t(f,g)=3 B_t(f,g)+J_t(f',g)+J_t(f,g'). Integrate in time and divide by three to obtain the normal-form identity with both endpoints. Smooth spatial Fourier series and their derivatives converge absolutely, justifying the differentiation. J is symmetric. In J_t(B_t(f,g),h), Dinv B_t(f,g)=S_(-t)P[(S_t f)(S_t g)], since Dinv*partial_x=P. Substitution, without commuting any operator through a product, gives the stated Cint identity after integration. The calculation holds on each smooth time piece, so summing preserves both external endpoints. For time-independent f set g=f and divide the integral by two; this yields Stage(t;f)=[J_s(f,f)]/6.
